{"id": "4:28/q07", "question": "What weakness was the human created with?", "turns_on": "Whether weakness is chiefly sexual impatience, wider moral vulnerability, material origin or bodily frailty, dependence, impaired judgment, or an inward capacity.", "positions": [{"id": "4:28/q07/p1", "position": "People have little patience to resist sexual desire, especially for women.", "reasons": "Muqatil and Tabari connect this with the slave-marriage concession preventing fornication; Salama singles out intercourse itself as the weakest moment, and Waki says reason departs around women. Tawus says no sphere makes a person weaker. Saʿid ibn al-Musayyib fears temptation even at eighty with failing sight, and ʿUbada fears Satan if alone with an unlawful woman despite wealth and frailty (Thalabi, Qurtubi); Alusi reports a saying that even a noble man is overcome by women. Tabatabai describes implanted sexual powers continually pressing toward their objects; Kuran Yolu treats sexual desire as a vulnerability directed into lawful satisfaction."}, {"id": "4:28/q07/p2", "position": "People are broadly vulnerable to desire, appetite, passion, anger, fear and grief, and struggle with demanding obedience.", "reasons": "Zajjaj, Ibn Kaysan, Nahhas and Qurtubi mention desire and appetite, with Ibn Kaysan adding fear and grief; Kashshaf and Nasafi add hardship of worship. Al-Qadi (in Razi) stresses strong motives toward pleasure rather than weak bodily capacity; Razi accepts that account while disputing its Muʿtazilite implication. Alusi reports these variants; Bursevi adds unreliable control of appetites and powers. Kuran Yolu adds love of wealth, warning of its corruption while encouraging lawful earning."}, {"id": "4:28/q07/p3", "position": "Human weakness lies in being created from lowly fluid or another frail beginning.", "reasons": "Al-Hasan cites 30:54; Ibn al-Jawzi also identifies daʿf in 30:54 as semen. Raghib relates weakness to humanity's beginning and end. Alusi rejects the weak-substance explanation as poorly fitted to the marriage context."}, {"id": "4:28/q07/p4", "position": "People are weak in judgment and reason unless God grants certainty and light.", "reasons": "Sulami says strength comes through certainty, not the self; Alusi reports that divine light alone discloses hidden wisdom, but calls this poorly supported by the marriage context."}, {"id": "4:28/q07/p5", "position": "Weakness means poverty, need and dependence on God and one another.", "reasons": "Qushayri treats need as an excuse. Biqai says people cannot abstain from marriage and other appetites or act without divine support. Raghib relates weakness to comparison with the celestial realm, the human apart from God's aid, or mutual dependence; he balances this with human intellect, vicegerency, nearness to God, and God's favor in 17:70."}, {"id": "4:28/q07/p6", "position": "It is physical frailty, shown by pain from even a small event.", "reasons": "Alusi reports this from al-Hasan but rejects it as ill suited to the marriage context."}, {"id": "4:28/q07/p7", "position": "People cannot endure a moment's separation from God; this weakness reflects divine and human mutual love.", "reasons": "Bursevi praises this spiritual weakness as a mark peculiar to humans. Alusi says humans cannot endure a moment's veil from the beloved or separation from the desired. He holds that patience with God is blameworthy because of perfect longing, though patience otherwise is praiseworthy. He reports al-Shibli's prayer that there is no rest with God and no escape from Him, seeking refuge through God in God."}, {"id": "4:28/q07/p8", "position": "Weakness is human mutability between animal appetite and angelic obedience, with potential for either misery or perfection.", "reasons": "Bursevi says this capacity belongs uniquely to humans, permits perfection through adopting divine attributes, and makes the perfected human best of creation or the beastly human worst. He cites a divine hadith promising the obedient a living kingship without death."}, {"id": "4:28/q07/p9", "position": "Humans cannot bear unseen disclosures or the force of witnessing without divine aid.", "reasons": "Alusi gives this as an inward account of human weakness."}]}
{"id": "4:28/q08", "question": "What is the lexical sense and range of ḍaʿīf?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:28/q08/p1", "position": "It denotes weakness, the opposite or absence of strength; here it can mean little patience or inability to restrain desire.", "reasons": "Jishumi treats weakness and lightness as absences of strength and heaviness rather than independent qualities. Ibn al-Jawzi derives ḍaʿīf from ḍaʿf and gives the noun's two vocalizations, ḍaʿf and ḍuʿf; he glosses this verse as little patience and catalogues other contexts: incapacitated (4:76, 8:66), blind (11:91), chronically infirm (9:91), oppressed (28:5), socially lowly (34:31), and semen (30:54)."}]}
{"id": "4:28/q09", "question": "How is ḍaʿīfan parsed in 'the human was created weak'?", "turns_on": "The function of the final accusative and whether khalaqa can take a second object or an omitted 'from' phrase.", "positions": [{"id": "4:28/q09/p1", "position": "It is an accusative circumstance describing the human, emphatic on the usual passive reading and also possible on the active reading.", "reasons": "Nahhas, Ibn Atiyya, Qurtubi, Abu Hayyan, Samīn and Alusi give the circumstantial parse. Abu Hayyan and Samīn reject a proposed tamyīz or specification parse, though they differ in how they discuss supplying min."}, {"id": "4:28/q09/p2", "position": "It is understood through an omitted preposition and qualified noun: created from a weak substance.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan mentions clay or embryonic stages; Samīn gives lowly water or a drop. Alusi says this does not fit the context."}, {"id": "4:28/q09/p3", "position": "On the active reading, it is a second object if khalaqa is taken like jaʿala.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya proposes this; Abu Hayyan objects that no grammarian makes khalaqa govern two objects this way, and Samīn calls it unusual because jaʿala meaning 'create' takes one object."}, {"id": "4:28/q09/p4", "position": "It is a tamyīz or specification accusative.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan and Samīn report and reject this proposal; the possibility of inserting min is discussed."}]}
{"id": "4:28/q10", "question": "How is khuliqa read?", "turns_on": "Whether the verb is passive or active, changing the grammatical subject and case of al-insān.", "positions": [{"id": "4:28/q10/p1", "position": "The majority read passive khuliqa, with al-insān as the passive subject.", "reasons": "Nahhas calls the verb passive; Ibn Atiyya explicitly contrasts the majority reading with the active variant."}, {"id": "4:28/q10/p2", "position": "Ibn Abbas, and in some transmissions Mujahid, read active khalaqa: God created the human weak.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan include Mujahid; Kashshaf, Qurtubi and Alusi name Ibn Abbas. Al-insān is accusative and God's name is the understood subject; Ibn Atiyya keeps ḍaʿīfan circumstantial or proposes a second object."}]}
{"id": "4:28/q11", "question": "How does human weakness explain God's easing?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:28/q11/p1", "position": "The coordinating clause gives the reason for concessions: weak people struggle under severe obligations, especially marriage restrictions.", "reasons": "Nahhas and Qurtubi connect easily swayed desire with necessary concessions. Biqai makes the waw causal. Ibn Ashur calls the second clause a concluding generalization explaining the first; Islam is suited to all times and places whereas earlier religions addressed particular conditions, and 8:66 similarly cites known weakness before relief. Elmalili says legislation must avoid both indulgence of lust and oppressive severity; easier marriage and dealings avert fornication and misuse. Kuran Yolu says obligations have concessions in normal and exceptional circumstances. Tabatabai says the cause is general but impediments kept its effects from earlier peoples until repentance and mercy reached this community."}, {"id": "4:28/q11/p2", "position": "God eases servanthood through witnessing or delight in worship because humans cannot bear spiritual disclosure unaided or separation from God.", "reasons": "Alusi gives witnessing and delight after patience as ways God eases the burden (r8), and describes human inability to bear disclosure or separation (r9)."}]}
{"id": "4:28/q12", "question": "Does the verse rule out obligations beyond human capacity or support a view of who creates human acts?", "turns_on": "Whether the need for divine easing is compatible with God creating acts and the motives behind them.", "positions": [{"id": "4:28/q12/p1", "position": "God's stated wish to ease rules out duties beyond capacity and human acts created by God.", "reasons": "Al-Qadi argues that creating unbelief then forbidding it, or withholding faith while commanding it, would impose the greatest burden. Razi rejects the argument by invoking prior replies from divine knowledge and motivating causes."}, {"id": "4:28/q12/p2", "position": "The motives that move people to act ultimately come from God.", "reasons": "Razi accepts al-Qadi's analysis of motives but argues that their causes must either regress infinitely or originate with God; he calls the latter correct and says it defeats al-Qadi's Muʿtazilite position."}]}
{"id": "4:28/q13", "question": "What legal guidance follows from the verse's promise of ease?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:28/q13/p1", "position": "Religious obligations should be manageable, with concessions for hardship while lawful routes channel desire and protect benefits.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur calls ease foundational and says the law can accept a lesser harm to prevent hardship or secure benefit, including slave marriage; he says two kinds of concessions branch from it. Elmalili rules out excessive severity and

{"id": "4:28/q14", "question": "How does this verse connect to its surrounding passage and other verses about ease?", "turns_on": "Which part of the surrounding passage supplies the link: prior divine intentions, the marriage rule, or the subsequent financial address.", "positions": [{"id": "4:28/q14/p1", "position": "It follows God's clarification and repentance in 4:26–27 and states enduring care and ease for the community.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur links it to 4:26 and sees its human-weakness statement as a concluding rationale. He compares 8:66, where God lightens a burden knowing believers' weakness. Elmalili and Tabatabai connect the prayer against heavy burdens in 2:286 with 7:157, 2:185 and 22:78. Study Quran also cites 2:185; Asad describes integrated spiritual and bodily guidance."}, {"id": "4:28/q14/p2", "position": "It leads from marriage and inheritance to financial conduct, because marriage depends on means and wealth management protects lineage.", "reasons": "Biqai says human weakness undermines denying women and minors inheritance and explains the move toward rules for money. Elmalili links the next address, 4:29, to the financial ability needed for marriage and the handling of wealth."}, {"id": "4:28/q14/p3", "position": "Nearby wording about human weakness signals why the conditional slave-marriage rule addresses sexual desire.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan notes a series of implied links: reluctance suggests consensual inheritance transfer, restrictions on coercing wives can serve their benefit, the prohibition on fathers' wives recalls pre-Islamic custom, a permission implies an earlier ban, and slave-marriage conditions and weakness signal desire."}]}
{"id": "4:28/q15", "question": "What is reported about the value of this verse among verses of al-Nisāʾ?", "turns_on": "The transmitted enumeration of the eight verses, whose last entries differ across sources.", "positions": [{"id": "4:28/q15/p1", "position": "Ibn Abbas counted it among eight verses better for this community than everything under the sun, usually alongside 4:26, 4:27, 4:31, 4:40, 4:48, 4:110 and 4:147.", "reasons": "Thalabi gives this list; Kashshaf gives the first three as clarification, repentance and relief and names 4:31 and 4:48; Durr gives only an excerpt; Study Quran names the same eight and calls them signs of mercy. Elmalili's listed references include 4:116 as well as 4:147, producing a variant enumeration."}, {"id": "4:28/q15/p2", "position": "A transmitted list substitutes 4:116 and 3:147 for 4:48 and 4:147.", "reasons": "Razi gives this enumeration and then prays to be worthy of the blessings of these verses by grace and mercy."}, {"id": "4:28/q15/p3", "position": "A transmitted list substitutes 4:152 for 4:147.", "reasons": "Alusi attributes this list to al-Bayhaqi from Ibn Abbas."}]}
{"id": "4:28/q16", "question": "What rhetorical qualities does the verse exemplify?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:28/q16/p1", "position": "Its wording exemplifies the Qur'an's gentle register, suited to its context.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur contrasts this register with a forceful warning in 41:13 and also cites 39:53 for gentleness. In his wider discussion he describes taḍmīn as a dependent showing a verb's additional sense; unusually effective Qur'anic proverbial expression (39:39, 4:81, 41:34, surpassing Zuhayr); expansive description that instills fear, illustrated by Ibn Ziyaba's poetry (75:26–29, 56:83–84, 14:43); and concise simultaneous literal and figurative senses where context permits. These are general rhetorical comparisons, not claims that each device occurs in this verse."}]}
{"id": "4:28/q17", "question": "What does the related phrase 'do not kill yourselves' mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:28/q17/p1", "position": "It means do not destroy yourselves.", "reasons": "Abu Ubayda (Majaz) glosses the phrase lā taqtulū anfusakum this way."}]}
{"id": "4:105/q01", "question": "What is the Book sent down to the Prophet?", "turns_on": "Whether the Book is read as the Qurʾan in its outward sense or as knowledge of divine manifestations.", "positions": [{"id": "4:105/q01/p1", "position": "The Qurʾan, containing commands, prohibitions, rulings and guidance.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī identifies al-kitāb as the Qurʾan; al-Baghawī specifies commands, prohibitions and decisive judgment; Ibn Kathīr says its reports and commands are true; Elmalılı describes rights before God and people."}, {"id": "4:105/q01/p2", "position": "In an inward reading, the Book is detailed knowledge of divine attributes, their manifestations, and their rulings.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī grounds this knowledge in truth and justice and makes it the basis of judgment."}]}
{"id": "4:105/q02", "question": "What does sending the Book 'in truth' mean?", "turns_on": "Whether truth describes the Book's content and mode of revelation, its just purpose, or the Prophet's entitlement.", "positions": [{"id": "4:105/q02/p1", "position": "The Book is true, contains truth, and is revealed rightly, without falsehood or deviation.", "reasons": "Muqātil contrasts truth with vain revelation and cites 34:6. Al-Wāḥidī cites 22:62 for possessing truth. Al-Jishumī defines truth as putting things where wisdom requires and calls the Book ordered by wisdom. Al-Māturīdī includes protection from alteration and true reports, commands, rights and resurrection. Ibn Kathīr includes reports and commands."}, {"id": "4:105/q02/p2", "position": "It means revelation for just judgment and the fulfillment of rights.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī glosses al-ḥaqq as judgment with justice. Al-Ṭabrisī says God's due from servants; al-Māturīdī includes duties and mutual rights; Elmalılı describes fair settlement of doctrinal and practical disputes."}, {"id": "4:105/q02/p3", "position": "It may mean the Prophet is most entitled to the Book.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī and al-Ṭabrisī record this gloss."}]}
{"id": "4:105/q03", "question": "How does 'in truth' attach grammatically?", "turns_on": "Whether the preposition qualifies the Book as a state or the act of sending.", "positions": [{"id": "4:105/q03/p1", "position": "It is a circumstantial qualification: the Book was sent down clothed in truth.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn calls it emphatic; al-Ālūsī likewise makes it a state of the Qurʾan."}, {"id": "4:105/q03/p2", "position": "The preposition attaches to 'We sent down'; alternatively the Book descended upon and clarified truth.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī gives both parsings."}]}
{"id": "4:105/q04", "question": "Why is the opening expressed emphatically and with 'to you'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:105/q04/p1", "position": "The emphasis marks the ruling's importance, the majestic plural magnifies it, and placing the recipient early draws attention.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī gives these rhetorical functions."}, {"id": "4:105/q04/p2", "position": "The preposition ilā accompanies rational recipients in Qurʾanic usage, whereas ʿalā can accompany rational and inanimate recipients.", "reasons": "Al-Sāmarrāʾī draws this usage distinction."}]}
{"id": "4:105/q05", "question": "For what purpose was the Book sent down here?", "turns_on": "Whether the clause stresses the Book's provision of law or the Prophet's authority to apply it.", "positions": [{"id": "4:105/q05/p1", "position": "It enables the Prophet to judge disputes among all people by divine truth, rights, and rulings.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās calls the lām purposive; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī compares the general statement in 2:213. Al-Biqāʿī ties 'all people' to the universality of the Prophet's call; al-Ālūsī includes upright and wicked alike; Kur'an Yolu lists facts, norms, methods and general and specific rulings. Abū Ḥayyān says the verse honors the Messenger by entrusting judgment to him under divine direction."}, {"id": "4:105/q05/p2", "position": "The Prophet's particular judicial decisions themselves have binding authority.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī distinguishes this verse from 2:213: a concrete case requires determining which general rule applies, and this verse grants authority to the Prophet's judgment."}]}
{"id": "4:105/q06", "question": "What governs the purposive lām in 'so that you judge'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:105/q06/p1", "position": "It depends on 'We sent down' and states the purpose of revelation.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās calls it purposive; al-Samīn names anzalnā as governor."}]}
{"id": "4:105/q07", "question": "What does 'what God showed you' mean?", "turns_on": "Whether God's showing denotes revealed instruction, divinely guided reasoning, a particular judicial determination, evidentiary proof, or inward disclosure.", "positions": [{"id": "4:105/q07/p1", "position": "What God taught or disclosed through the Book and revelation.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba and al-Wāḥidī compare 34:6; al-Dāmghānī adds 2:128, 71:14 and 21:30. Ibn ʿAbbās and ʿAṭiyya specify the revealed Book. Al-Burūsawī calls this certain recognition 'seeing' for its clarity and force; al-Rāzī likens its certainty to vision. Al-Biqāʿī says the Prophet should act once God clarifies a matter and wait where it remains unclear, rather than follow whim."}, {"id": "4:105/q07/p2", "position": "What God inspired through reasoning from revealed principles, including the Prophet's own guided ijtihād.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī lists the Prophet's ijtihād; Ibn ʿAṭiyya combines explicit revelation and reasoning along its path; Abū Manṣūr and al-Māturīdī say God does not show him

 error; al-Rāzī says sound analogy remains obedience to scripture."}, {"id": "4:105/q07/p3", "position": "The divine determination of the right judgment in a concrete dispute, beyond knowledge of general laws.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says God formed the Prophet's judgment and added it to the Book's rules and wisdom."}, {"id": "4:105/q07/p4", "position": "Clear proofs and witnesses, or sound outward evidence used in adjudication.", "reasons": "Maṭar names proof and witnesses; Ibn al-Jawzī says the Prophet was taught to reject unproved claims; al-Biqāʿī says the judge need not inspect hidden states."}, {"id": "4:105/q07/p5", "position": "Direct unveiling or knowledge cast into the Prophet's heart, reaching past ordinary outward appearances.", "reasons": "Al-Sulamī reports unveiling and direct witnessing; Ibn ʿAṭā says the Prophet sees through God; Abū Ḥayyān records illuminated inner perception; al-Qāshānī calls it divine justice shown apart from the self."}]}
{"id": "4:105/q08", "question": "What are the lexical and grammatical grounds for 'showed you'?", "turns_on": "Which sense and transitivity of raʾā underlie the causative form.", "positions": [{"id": "4:105/q08/p1", "position": "Arāka is a causative cognitive verb with two objects: the suffix and an omitted 'what'; it is not ocular seeing.", "reasons": "Abū ʿAlī says judgment cannot be seen by the eye and causativizing a two-object verb would require three objects. Al-Samīn and al-Ālūsī give the omitted relative pronoun. Al-Bayḍāwī rejects a three-object 'made you know' analysis, while al-Ālūsī calls derivation from opinion remote."}, {"id": "4:105/q08/p2", "position": "The root's senses extend from visual perception to knowledge, consideration, hearing, wonder, and informing.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī contrasts visual examples (39:60, 63:4, 76:20), reflection (16:79), hearing (6:68), wonder (4:49, 4:60), informing (2:258, 105:1), and related forms for opinion, fullness, report transmission, ostentation and poetic rhyme. Here he selects knowledge/instruction."}, {"id": "4:105/q08/p3", "position": "Deriving arāka from raʾā 'to hold an opinion' is possible, with one object before causativization and two after.", "reasons": "Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī offers this parsing; al-Samīn also permits opinion or knowledge. Al-Ālūsī objects that an opinion verb should take three objects here, with two suppressed."}]}
{"id": "4:105/q09", "question": "May the Prophet judge by ijtihād?", "turns_on": "Whether divine showing confines judgment to direct revelation or includes guided reasoning from it.", "positions": [{"id": "4:105/q09/p1", "position": "Yes: his ijtihād applies and extends revealed principles under God's guidance.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī, Abū Manṣūr, al-Māturīdī and some legal theorists cite this verse. Ibn ʿAṭiyya allows reasoned judgment following revelation. Ibn Kathīr cites the inheritance dispute and Abū Dāwūd's wording that the Prophet judged by opinion where no revelation had arrived. Kur'an Yolu says divine oversight corrects mistakes; al-Rāzī defends text-grounded analogy against its denial."}, {"id": "4:105/q09/p2", "position": "His judgments are wholly based on revelation or explicit text, not independent opinion.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī reports al-Ḥasan's assertion that prophets' judgments are revelation; Ibn ʿAbbās warns against personal opinion. ʿUmar says only the Prophet can call a judgment what God showed him, ordinary opinions being conjecture. Al-Rāzī records an inference against analogy from 7:158 but answers that authorized analogy itself follows scripture; Kur'an Yolu explicitly rejects using this verse to deny prophetic ijtihād."}]}
{"id": "4:105/q10", "question": "How should judges decide when the facts are disputed?", "turns_on": "Whether the case is governed by conclusive knowledge, ordinary proof, or reasoned judgment where text is silent.", "positions": [{"id": "4:105/q10/p1", "position": "They should use proof, witnesses, and what they hear, without accepting an unsupported accusation or favoring a persuasive wrongdoer.", "reasons": "Maṭar names clear proofs and witnesses; Ibn al-Jawzī says no claim against another without proof; al-Biqāʿī says outward evidence is sufficient. Umm Salama's report warns that a skilled claimant may win another's right, a piece of fire. Kur'an Yolu says a proper judge may err through deceptive testimony and the deceivers bear the responsibility. Elmalılı requires investigation and forbids a ruling against certain known facts."}, {"id": "4:105/q10/p2", "position": "When no explicit text settles the case, qualified reasoning is available, but presumptuous judgment without knowledge is unreliable.", "reasons": "Mālik distinguishes binding Qurʾan and established Sunna, potentially correct qualified reasoning, and unsupported presumption. The Prophet's inheritance dispute ended with division, a lot, and mutual release; Abū Dāwūd says he judged by opinion where revelation had not come."}]}
{"id": "4:105/q11", "question": "What does 'traitors' mean lexically?", "turns_on": "Whether khiyāna is limited here to breach of deposit, encompasses wrongful taking, or signals an inward trust.", "positions": [{"id": "4:105/q11/p1", "position": "Those who fail a trust; betrayal is the opposite of trustworthiness and has a root sense of diminution.", "reasons": "Al-Dāmghānī applies breach of trust to the armor; al-Jishumī gives deficiency or taking away; Ibn al-Jawzī adds takhawwan for shortchanging and Thaʿlab's possible derivation of khuwān. Ibn al-Jawzī catalogs other Qurʾanic uses: disobedience (2:187, 8:27, 40:19), covenant breaking (5:13, 8:58), religious disloyalty (4:107, 8:71, 66:10), adultery (12:52)."}, {"id": "4:105/q11/p2", "position": "In this context, betrayal includes theft and any wrongful violation of another's rights, including the community's shared trust.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī argues that the context points to theft and similar violations, since believers form one self; he prefers this to narrowing it to deposits. Al-Ṭabarī prefers the deposit account on the lexical ground that theft is not betrayal in the same proper sense."}, {"id": "4:105/q11/p3", "position": "In an inward reading, they betray the primordial trust of knowing God and misuse rights entrusted to their capacities.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī extends betrayal of self and others to failure of that trust."}]}
{"id": "4:105/q12", "question": "Who are 'the traitors' in the verse?", "turns_on": "Whether the plural names the accused household and accomplices, all people acting similarly, or hypocrites as a class.", "positions": [{"id": "4:105/q12/p1", "position": "Ṭuʿma or Abū Ṭuʿma of Banū Ubayriq/Ẓafar and those who defended him.", "reasons": "Muqātil and al-Baghawī name him; al-Wāḥidī, Abū Ḥayyān, al-Burūsawī, al-Ālūsī and Elmalılı include his helpers. Abū Ḥayyān explains the plural by three brothers and those who knowingly vouched for the thief; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī's Qatāda report calls Banū Ubayriq the traitors."}, {"id": "4:105/q12/p2", "position": "The warning extends to anyone who commits such treachery or injustice.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān makes the plural general; al-Ṭabrisī includes betrayals against Muslims or protected non-Muslims in person or property; Elmalılı and Asad likewise generalize the admonition."}, {"id": "4:105/q12/p3", "position": "The traitors can be read as hypocrites in the larger passage, without confining the point to one incident.", "reasons": "Ibn Baḥr links it to 4:88; Elmalılı says this can accord with the reported Ṭuʿma incident, since he was a hypocrite."}]}
{"id": "4:105/q13", "question": "What does 'be a disputant for the traitors' forbid?", "turns_on": "Whether the prohibition concerns human advocacy in a dispute or an inward plea against divine justice.", "positions": [{"id": "4:105/q13/p1", "position": "Do not advocate a traitor's false claim against an innocent or rightful party, even across religious lines.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj and al-Wāḥidī gloss it as litigating or defending; al-Kashshāf specifies Banū Ẓafar against the Jew. Al-Ṭabrisī includes protected non-Muslims. Ibn al-Jawzī says advocacy requires knowing the facts. Elmalılı and Kur'an Yolu extend the rule to judges, witnesses and lawyers, against bias from rank, wealth, fame, gain or collusion; legitimate advocacy protects rightful claims, settlement and fair penalties."}, {"id": "4:105/q13/p2", "position": "In the inward sense, do not plead for traitors against divine punishment or say that God wronged them.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī says wrongdoers have no defense against the consequences of their acts."}]}

{"id": "4:105/q15", "question": "How are the lām and omitted complement in the prohibition construed?", "turns_on": "Whether the preposition retains its ordinary benefactive sense or is read by substitution.", "positions": [{"id": "4:105/q15/p1", "position": "The lām means 'on behalf of' the traitors; the omitted complement is the innocent person or pleading the accused's innocence.", "reasons": "Al-Rāghib compares 4:107 and distinguishes 'adversary of God'; al-Samīn says the normal lām suffices without replacing it with ʿan. Abū Ḥayyān supplies pleading innocence; al-Samīn supplies 'the innocent.'"}, {"id": "4:105/q15/p2", "position": "The preposition may instead mean 'away from' or 'concerning' them.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī records these alternatives without preferring them."}]}

not be' connected to the preceding sentence?", "turns_on": "Whether the prohibition continues an implied command or needs another syntactic coordination.", "positions": [{"id": "4:105/q16/p1", "position": "It follows an implicit command drawn from the declaration: judge by the Book, and do not advocate for traitors.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī prefers an omitted command; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī treats the declarative clause itself as commanding judgment."}, {"id": "4:105/q16/p2", "position": "It can be coordinated with 'We sent down' by supplying 'We said', or with 'the Book' as another revealed injunction.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī records these possibilities and calls the latter remote."}]}
{"id": "4:105/q17", "question": "What happened in the theft case behind the revelation?", "turns_on": "Whether the underlying charge was theft of armor, betrayal of a deposited item, the Rifāʿa storeroom theft, or a general hypocrite context.", "positions": [{"id": "4:105/q17/p1", "position": "Ṭuʿma stole armor from Qatāda or his household, hid it with the Jew Zayd, and his clan urged the Prophet to blame the Jew.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās versions give a leaking flour or bran sack leading to Zayd ibn al-Samīn; some say the Prophet nearly ordered the Jew's hand cut off. Al-Bayḍāwī and al-Nasafī mention Ṭuʿma's oath and Jewish witnesses. Al-Burūsawī says the clan knowingly conspired overnight; Elmalılı prefers this majority account. Names and minor details vary. Elmalılı reports consensus on the Banū Ubayriq occasion and al-Kirmānī's identification of Ṭuʿma as of Banū Ẓafar ibn al-Ḥārith. Elmalılı transmits al-Rāzī's statement that most of the verses concern Ṭuʿma, while case details differ. Ibn Kathīr reports Ibn ʿAbbās's version in which Ṭuʿma hid a stolen shield in an innocent man's house and his clan sought public defense. Ibn Kathīr says Mujāhid, ʿIkrima, Qatāda, al-Suddī and Ibn Zayd relate the thief's occasion with variations. Al-Ḥasan and Ibn Zayd say Ṭuʿma stole armor and relatives argued for him."}, {"id": "4:105/q17/p2", "position": "Armor had been entrusted to Ṭuʿma, who denied the deposit, concealed it in another house, and implicated an innocent party.", "reasons": "Muqātil says Zayd entrusted it and Ṭuʿma hid it with Abū Malik; al-Suddī's reports name Abū Malil/Mulayl. Other versions have an Anṣārī depositor, a Jew as owner or party, and a false charge against that Jew. Al-Ṭabarī prefers this account because betrayal properly describes violation of a deposit."}, {"id": "4:105/q17/p3", "position": "Banū Ubayriq broke into Rifāʿa's store and stole food and weapons, then falsely blamed the upright Muslim Labīd and attacked Qatāda's accusation.", "reasons": "Qatāda names three brothers, Bishr, Bashīr and Mubashshir; reports variously name Rifāʿa ibn Zayd and his nephew Qatāda, two armors and swords, or food and a single armor. Bashīr was a hypocritical poet who falsely attributed anti-Companion verse. Usayr ibn ʿUrwa rallied neighbors; the Prophet rebuked Qatāda for accusing a pious household without proof; revelation exposed them and the weapons were returned. Ibn ʿAṭiyya says commentators agree that the Banū Ubayriq case prompted the warning and command to seek forgiveness. Qatāda and other interpreters identify the culprit as Taʿma, also called Tuʿayma."}, {"id": "4:105/q17/p4", "position": "The passage concerns hypocrites generally, continuing the earlier division over them.", "reasons": "Ibn Baḥr links it to 4:88; Elmalılı says the named culprit's hypocrisy can reconcile the accounts. Asad objects to treating the ethical teaching as exclusively historical."}]}
{"id": "4:105/q18", "question": "Who was the innocent person accused in the reported case?", "turns_on": "The accused person's identity follows the differing occasion reports.", "positions": [{"id": "4:105/q18/p1", "position": "A Jew, usually named Zayd ibn al-Samīn, with reported variants of his name.", "reasons": "The flour-sack accounts identify him as the recipient of planted armor; al-Ṭabrisī has Zayd ibn al-Suhaym, while al-Māwardī records Yazīd ibn al-Samak."}, {"id": "4:105/q18/p2", "position": "Abū Malik or Abū Malil al-Anṣārī, in the entrusted-armor version.", "reasons": "Al-Suddī says Ṭuʿma hid the deposited armor in his house and tried to frame him."}, {"id": "4:105/q18/p3", "position": "The upright Anṣārī Labīd ibn Sahl, in the Rifāʿa storeroom version.", "reasons": "Banū Ubayriq named him as thief; al-Māwardī lists him among accounts of the person involved."}]}
{"id": "4:105/q19", "question": "Did the Prophet actually defend the accused traitor before revelation?", "turns_on": "Whether the Prophet acted, merely intended to act, or rebuked an accuser on the apparent evidence.", "positions": [{"id": "4:105/q19/p1", "position": "He defended him or publicly argued for him on the apparent evidence.", "reasons": "Al-ʿAwfī from Ibn ʿAbbās says he rose to defend him; al-Ḍaḥḥāk's account says he defended the apparently innocent depositor after relatives pleaded. Al-Māwardī's account says he argued or was about to argue."}, {"id": "4:105/q19/p2", "position": "He intended or inclined to defend him, but revelation intervened before any defense or judgment.", "reasons": "Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and Qatāda say intention only; al-Ṭabrisī says the reproach addressed intention. Many flour-sack reports say he nearly supported Ṭuʿma or punished the Jew. Al-Rāzī says he waited for revelation; al-Burūsawī says he withheld judgment. Ibn ʿAṭiyya criticizes his quick acceptance of the report."}, {"id": "4:105/q19/p3", "position": "In the Qatāda report, he reproached Qatāda for an unsupported accusation before revelation exposed the household.", "reasons": "Qatāda says the Prophet rebuked him on the clan's representation; the later command to seek forgiveness is related to that rebuke in his gloss."}]}
{"id": "4:105/q20", "question": "What does the correction imply about prophetic protection from error?", "turns_on": "Whether the warning proves a completed wrong act, an excused intention, or a lesson to the community.", "positions": [{"id": "4:105/q20/p1", "position": "The warning does not establish a sinful defense: God protected or corrected the Prophet before a wrong judgment.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī says a prohibition is no proof the act occurred; possible forgiveness concerns inclination toward an apparent Muslim, an excused intent based on false testimony, or seeking forgiveness for the defenders. Ibn ʿAṭiyya and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī affirm protection; Abū Ḥayyān says his protection explains why the address instructs others. Kur'an Yolu distinguishes infallible conveyance from fallible fact-finding corrected by God."}, {"id": "4:105/q20/p2", "position": "Some take his intended defense and the forgiveness command as a possible challenge to protection from major sins.", "reasons": "Study Quran reports this inference from the warnings; al-Rāzī rejects the claim that the prohibition proves a forbidden act."}]}
{"id": "4:105/q21", "question": "What became of the accused thief after the revelation?", "turns_on": "The reports give different endings for the fugitive.", "positions": [{"id": "4:105/q21/p1", "position": "He fled to Mecca, apostatized, and died when a wall or house collapsed during burglary.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj, al-Kashshāf, al-Rāzī and Ibn Zayd transmit this ending; other accounts mention his lodging with Sulāfa and expulsion after Ḥassān's satire. The associated warning is linked to 4:115. Al-Ālūsī reports Ḥassān's satire of Sulāfa and her casting the fugitive's possessions at al-Abṭaḥ. Al-Māwardī records Ṭuʿma's apostasy and flight to Meccan polytheists, connected to 4:115. Al-Ṭabrisī reports the woman carrying his load to al-Abṭaḥ, throwing it down, and complaining in connection with Ḥassān's poem."}, {"id": "4:105/q21/p2", "position": "After fleeing and theft, he was expelled or killed by people he robbed, variously at Banū Sulaym or after a Qudāʿa caravan robbery.", "reasons": "Al-Suddī places his death at a lava field after al-Ḥajjāj expelled him; ʿIkrima says a stone first struck him and a caravan later stoned him; Ibn ʿAṭiyya lists killing by Arabs."}, {"id": "4:105/q21/p3", "position": "He sailed toward Jeddah, stole a purse aboard ship, and was thrown into the sea.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī records this alternative."}]}
{"id": "4:105/q22", "question": "How is the Banū Ubayriq report graded?", "turns_on": "Whether the connected route's rarity or an authenticity grading bears more weight.", "positions": [{"id": "4:105/q22/p1", "position": "It is gharīb as a connected report; other transmissions are mursal.", "reasons": "Al-Tirmidhī says Muḥammad ibn Salamah alone transmits a connected chain while Yūnus ibn Bukayr and others omit Qatāda's father and grandfather. Ibn Kathīr calls an Ibn ʿAbbās story unusual."}, {"id": "4:105/q22/p2", "position": "Al-Ḥākim grades Qatāda's report sound by Muslim's criteria, though neither major Ṣaḥīḥ includes it.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr and al-Suyūṭī transmit al-Ḥākim's assessment; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī notes it and says the basic story has many routes with slight variations, though he cautions that occasion reports may apply remembered events to similar verses."}]}
{"id": "4:105/q23", "question": "How does the passage relate to its context and other verses?", "turns_on": "Which surrounding theme supplies the immediate transition and how the local case illustrates broader scriptural principles.", "positions": [{"id": "4:105/q23/p1", "position": "It returns from discussion of hypocrites and fighting to their attempt to corrupt judgment; even unbelief cannot justify injustice.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī gives this sequence and the connection to fighting disbelievers; Abū Ḥayyān and al-Ṭabrisī similarly describe the return to hypocrites. Al-Biqāʿī ties it to the People of the Book and hypocrites seeking another judgment and to exposing hidden opponents."}, {"id": "4:105/q23/p2", "position": "After many laws, it affirms their divine truth and requires judgment

by them rather than pleasing a group.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī and al-Ṭabrisī give this connection; Abū Ḥayyān emphasizes that even an unbeliever receives revealed justice."}, {"id": "4:105/q23/p3", "position": "It applies the general principle of 2:213 to a particular case and gives the Prophet authoritative judgment.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the whole passage forms a unit requiring judicial justice and lived religion."}, {"id": "4:105/q23/p4", "position": "Its command against defense of traitors is reinforced later in the passage by 4:107–113 and 4:109.", "reasons": "Al-Rāghib compares 4:107; Kur'an Yolu cites 4:109; Study Quran connects betrayal of others with betrayal of oneself, and with verses saying people wrong themselves (2:57, 3:117, 7:160)."}]}
{"id": "4:105/q24", "question": "Who is instructed by the warning beyond its immediate addressee?", "turns_on": "Whether the prohibition is confined to the narrated event or governs later people generally.", "positions": [{"id": "4:105/q24/p1", "position": "The Prophet is addressed, and the community and later judges also learn a general rule.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī and Abū Ḥayyān say the address teaches others because the Prophet is protected. {"id": "4:105/q25", "question": "What broader purposes and methods of revelation are drawn from this verse?", "turns_on": "Which wider scriptural functions the cited authors use the verse to illustrate.", "positions": [{"id": "4:105/q25/p1", "position": "Revelation supplies law and moral guidance, and the Sunna explains its principles.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr urges Muslims to learn and teach scripture rather than neglect it like earlier People of the Book, and ranks Qurʾan-by-Qurʾan then Sunna interpretation, citing 16:44 and 16:64. Al-Shāfiʿī says the Prophet's rulings were understood from the Qurʾan; a prophetic report calls the Sunna a non-recited revelation. Al-Suyūṭī adds eyewitness Companion reports, reconciliation of transmitted differences, and sound interpretive commitments."}, {"id": "4:105/q25/p2", "position": "The Qurʾan's purposes also include moral refinement, general and detailed legislation, communal order, sound reasoning, knowledge, exhortation, and narrative instruction.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr cites 68:4 and ʿĀʾisha on the Prophet's Qurʾanic character; a report on perfecting noble character; Abū Khirāsh's poem on Islamic restraint; 5:48, 16:89 and 5:3 for legislation and complete principles; al-Shāṭibī on concise comprehensiveness; 3:103, 6:159, 8:46 and 42:38 on communal order; 2:269, 29:43, 39:9 and 68:1 on reasoning and learning; 12:3, 6:90 and 14:45 on exemplary stories; and 10:38 on the challenge of inimitability. He notes occasions clarify rhetoric and credits al-Ghazālī's survey. Ibn Kathīr links reviving dead earth to softening hardened hearts through faith, citing 57:16–17 as warning and encouragement."}, {"id": "4:105/q25/p3", "position": "Inwardly, revelation and judgment disclose divine justice and the trust of knowing God.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī reads the Book as knowledge of attributes and their manifestations; the Prophet judges by divine justice; betrayers fail the primordial trust."}, {"id": "4:105/q25/p4", "position": "Al-Khiḍr was a prophet, and Muhammad received all prophets' miracles plus miracles unique to him.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī calls the majority view that al-Khiḍr was a prophet sound and cites Ibn Ḥajar."}]}
{"id": "4:105/q26", "question": "What rhetorical or figurative features are noted around this verse?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:105/q26/p1", "position": "The passage uses unspecified referents, ellipsis, word correspondence, and figurative attribution.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān finds the referents of 'what God showed' and 'what you did not know' left unspecified, plus ellipses, repetitions with changed complements, similar forms such as yuḍillūka/y uḍillūna and ʿallamaka/taʿlam, and metaphors for travel and battle. Al-Jurjānī distinguishes rational attribution metaphor from transferred predicate metaphor: poetry assigns life to wealth and weapons and destruction to coins; 35:9 assigns life to rain-revived earth. {"id": "4:105/q27", "question": "Is assimilation of mīm into bāʾ in the verse accepted?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:105/q27/p1", "position": "Al-Ḥasan and Abū ʿAmr are reported to assimilate mīm into bāʾ, but grammarians disallow it because mīm is nasalized.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās records both the reading and grammatical objection."}]}
{"id": "4:113/q01", "question": "How does this verse connect to the surrounding defense of the accused?", "turns_on": "Whether the immediate case exhausts the wording.", "positions": [{"id": "4:113/q01/p1", "position": "It continues the warning against defending traitors and explains that revelation saved the Prophet from their advocates.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari and Ibn Ashur link it to 4:105; Biqai says the warning now turns to God's favor; Study Quran invokes 4:105 and 4:111; Tirmidhi links the case to 4:114."}, {"id": "4:113/q01/p2", "position": "It broadens the particular case into a standing warning and promise of protection.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya makes the wording general beyond Tu'ma's case; Abu Hayyan likewise sees anyone among the people attempting deception."}]}
{"id": "4:113/q02", "question": "What are God's opening favor and mercy to the Prophet?", "turns_on": "Whether the gifts name revelation in this case, prophetic office and protection, or a wider divine grace.", "positions": [{"id": "4:113/q02/p1", "position": "Revelation disclosed the plot and the true facts, protecting him from being misled.", "reasons": "Muqatil says the Quran clarified Tu'ma's case; Tabari says God guided him away from defending the traitor; Zajjaj and Nahhas stress the truth disclosed; Kashshaf adds gracious care; Baydawi specifies the addressee is the Messenger; Nasafi's wording about discovering the secret differs; Ibn Ashur ties the favor to correct judgment. Ibn Atiyya says the verse shows the degree of protection; Alusi adds safeguarding; Ibn al-Jawzi transmits Muqatil's case-based gloss; Tabarsi says the plot was turned away."}, {"id": "4:113/q02/p2", "position": "Favor is prophethood and mercy is protection from sin or judgment error.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas via Ata, Razi, and Elmalili give the paired gloss; Kalbi specifies revelation as the aid; Study Quran reports special aid or isma and notes its broader prophetic doctrine."}, {"id": "4:113/q02/p3", "position": "They are Islam and the Quran.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas gives this paired gloss, transmitted by Tha'labi and Ibn al-Jawzi."}, {"id": "4:113/q02/p4", "position": "Favor is the Book's revelation; mercy is the Prophet's elevated cause and protection of his companions.", "reasons": "Biqai distinguishes the two gifts."}, {"id": "4:113/q02/p5", "position": "Favor is subtle divine support and mercy is God's blessing.", "reasons": "Al-Jubba'i gives this distinction."}, {"id": "4:113/q02/p6", "position": "They are special protection from neglecting God's rights and from people's schemes.", "reasons": "Qushayri describes encompassing divine preservation."}, {"id": "4:113/q02/p7", "position": "Favor is enabling support that unfolds latent perfection, and mercy is the eternal gift of absolute perfection.", "reasons": "Qashani offers this inward account."}, {"id": "4:113/q02/p8", "position": "The terms describe revealed guidance that also guards believers from serious error.", "reasons": "Study Quran cites 4:83 and 24:10,14,20,21, so the words need not name solely prophetic qualities."}]}
{"id": "4:113/q03", "question": "How is the phrase after lawlā parsed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:113/q03/p1", "position": "It is a nominative subject with an understood predicate.", "reasons": "Sibawayh supplies the omitted predicate, as reported by Nahhas and Qurtubi."}]}
{"id": "4:113/q04", "question": "Does 'a group would have intended' deny that the group actually tried?", "turns_on": "Whether lawlā negates intent itself, only effective intent, or has an omitted answer.", "positions": [{"id": "4:113/q04/p1", "position": "They did intend; the conditional negates the effect of their effort, or an effective resolve, rather than the historical attempt.", "reasons": "Farra reads an elided la-qad; Wahidi cites Farra and Zajjaj; Baydawi distinguishes attempt from success; Samīn explains an ineffective or religiously consequential intention; Bursevi expressly says only its effect is denied; Alusi reports the same problem and reads the denied intention as signaling no effect."}, {"id": "4:113/q04/p2", "position": "The lawlā answer is omitted; 'they certainly intended' is an independent or oath-like statement.", "reasons": "Abu al-Baqa supplies 'they would have misled you' and compares 24:10; Burhan similarly describes an oath-like preposed assertion. Samīn prefers the expressed answer instead."}, {"id": "4:113/q04/p3", "position": "The defenders did not intend deception because they believed their claim was right.", "reasons": "Al-Raghib, reported by Alusi, says the Muslims thought their conduct sound; Ibn Ashur reports a Banu Zufr account in which the complainants believed Banu Ubayriq."}, {"id": "4:113/q04/p4", "position": "The group did not even firmly intend the deception.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur says the apparent wording denies the attempt itself: Muhammad's honesty deterred a confident lie

{"id": "4:113/q05", "question": "What does hamm mean here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:113/q05/p1", "position": "It means intending or firmly resolving to do something.", "reasons": "Jishumi and Tabarsi cite himma as aspiration and hammām as a king of high aspiration; Baghawi says intent or resolve; Ibn Atiyya intensifies it as a consuming purpose; Ibn Ashur requires determination and confidence."}]}
{"id": "4:113/q06", "question": "Who was the group that tried to mislead the Prophet?", "turns_on": "The competing occasion reports and whether the group is named narrowly or generally.", "positions": [{"id": "4:113/q06/p1", "position": "Tu'ma's or Banu Ubayriq's supporters, including Banu Zafar, who advocated for the accused thief.", "reasons": "Mujahid names Ibn Bayriq's associates; Zajjaj says some knew the theft; Wahidi and Razi say they sought to blame the Jew; Kashshaf, Baydawi, Nasafi and Abu Hayyan name Banu Zafar, while Tabatabai relates them to 4:109."}, {"id": "4:113/q06/p2", "position": "They were Usayr or Asir ibn Urwa and companions.", "reasons": "Qatada ibn al-Nu'man gives the name and describes praise of Banu Ubayriq and reproach of his accusation; reports spell the name Usayr, Asir, or Usayd."}, {"id": "4:113/q06/p3", "position": "They were the Thaqif delegation seeking religious concessions.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas reports demands concerning al-Uzza; versions add exemption from conscription and tax, idols, or denial of resurrection."}, {"id": "4:113/q06/p4", "position": "They were hypocrites plotting to kill the Prophet.", "reasons": "Jishumi, Tabarsi and Abu Muslim report an unsuccessful assassination; 32:10 is offered for 'mislead' in the sense of destroy."}, {"id": "4:113/q06/p5", "position": "The wording can describe any would-be misleader among people.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan generalize the case."}, {"id": "4:113/q06/p6", "position": "They were unbelievers unable to injure his religion or erase his prophethood.", "reasons": "Jishumi gives this further identification."}]}
{"id": "4:113/q07", "question": "To whom does 'among them' refer?", "turns_on": "The antecedent adopted for the pronoun.", "positions": [{"id": "4:113/q07/p1", "position": "To Banu Zafar or the accused man's partisans.", "reasons": "Kashshaf says this follows if the faction is Banu Zafar; Abu Hayyan calls that apparent."}, {"id": "4:113/q07/p2", "position": "To people generally.", "reasons": "Kashshaf associates this with the hypocrite reading; Nasafi and Alusi also report the broader antecedent."}]}
{"id": "4:113/q08", "question": "What did the plotters seek to make the Prophet do?", "turns_on": "The occasion and the range of ḍalāl, from mistaken judgment to physical destruction.", "positions": [{"id": "4:113/q08/p1", "position": "Give a false or unjust judgment by defending the thief and accusing an innocent person.", "reasons": "Farra and Zajjaj gloss an error of judgment; accounts say the armor was placed with or blamed on a Jew; Tabari says testimony and disguise of facts drove the plea; Al-Tabari in Study Quran stresses 4:105's warning."}, {"id": "4:113/q08/p2", "position": "Turn him away from truth or revelation, including the revelation concerning idols.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzi gives the broader 'turn from truth'; Alusi reports an idols-related reading; Damghani says ḍalāl need not imply unbelief and compares David in 38:26."}, {"id": "4:113/q08/p3", "position": "Destroy or kill him.", "reasons": "Tabarsi compares 32:10 and 9:74; Alusi also cites the lost-in-the-earth usage of 32:10."}]}
{"id": "4:113/q09", "question": "What happened in the reported case behind this verse?", "turns_on": "The reports assign different incidents and vary in the theft narrative's names and sequel.", "positions": [{"id": "4:113/q09/p1", "position": "Banu Ubayriq or Tu'ma stole armor, shifted blame to an innocent Jew, and enlisted advocates; revelation exposed the lie.", "reasons": "Mujahid specifies an iron coat; Qatada's versions name Usayr or Asir and say he rebuked Qatada; Durr reports Lubayd as falsely accused, and reports Tu'ma's flight to Mecca and apostasy; Ikrima adds later theft, expulsion and death after robbing travelers; Ibn Zayd instead says the thief died under a collapsing house."}, {"id": "4:113/q09/p2", "position": "A Thaqif delegation sought allegiance conditioned on concessions; the Prophet refused.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas versions differ: no resurrection and retention of idols, a year honoring al-Uzza, or exemption from conscription and tax."}, {"id": "4:113/q09/p3", "position": "Hypocrites attempted to assassinate the Prophet, but God protected him.", "reasons": "Jishumi, Tabarsi and Abu Muslim transmit this account."}]}
{"id": "4:113/q10", "question": "How is the infinitive 'to mislead you' governed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:113/q10/p1", "position": "A governing bāʾ is omitted before the infinitive clause.", "reasons": "Samīn says the clause's case then follows a known grammatical dispute."}]}
{"id": "4:113/q11", "question": "Why do the schemers mislead only themselves?", "turns_on": "Whether the reflexive error is explained by their deeds and consequences or a primordial disposition.", "positions": [{"id": "4:113/q11/p1", "position": "Their sinful collusion and false testimony constitute their own error, whose punishment and harm return to them.", "reasons": "Tabari cites the command against aiding sin in 4:105; Zajjaj and Nahhas call their conduct the acts of the misguided; Wahidi, Razi and Abu Hayyan specify collusion, false testimony, and slander; Tabarsi says invitation to error itself counts as misguidance and its consequence may be everlasting punishment; Bursevi cites al-Sa'ib's line that the oppressor suffers first; Study Quran compares 4:111, 3:69 and 39:41. Ibn Abbas says the plotters injure only themselves and cannot remove the Prophet's office."}, {"id": "4:113/q11/p2", "position": "Their own primordial disposition toward wretchedness generates the misguidance; it cannot transfer to the Prophet.", "reasons": "Qashani gives the inward causal account."}, {"id": "4:113/q11/p3", "position": "The different meaning of this phrase discussed at 3:69 also applies here.", "reasons": "Tabatabai mentions this earlier sense only to say it does not fit the present context."}]}
{"id": "4:113/q12", "question": "How are the clauses about self-misguidance and harm joined?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:113/q12/p1", "position": "The first statement is parenthetical and the denial of harm is coordinated with it.", "reasons": "Alusi describes this as the construction of the two clauses."}]}
{"id": "4:113/q13", "question": "Why can they cause the Prophet no harm?", "turns_on": "Whether the assurance rests on divine preservation, valid reliance on outward evidence, or the false witness's own liability.", "positions": [{"id": "4:113/q13/p1", "position": "God protects, guides and supports him and exposes their plot, including in the future.", "reasons": "Tabari specifies divine disclosure and strengthening; Zajjaj adds support for true religion; Qushayri says divine might guards him; Qaffal and Abu Hayyan read a future promise; Biqai compares 5:67 and includes outward and inward safety; Alusi gives alternatives of protection from heretics or people. Ibn Abbas says God's choice of the Prophet for prophethood makes that office impossible for them to strip."}, {"id": "4:113/q13/p2", "position": "A judgment on the outward evidence would not have harmed him because hidden facts were unknown.", "reasons": "Kashshaf and Nasafi excuse the Prophet's apparent thought; Razi says judging by appearances is what the law commands; Baydawi and Bursevi deny any bias; Elmalili states the judge is not liable when contrary facts are unknown."}, {"id": "4:113/q13/p3", "position": "False testimony harms its giver, not the Prophet.", "reasons": "Wahidi identifies the false witness as the harmed party."}]}
{"id": "4:113/q14", "question": "How does 'min shayʾ' intensify the denial of harm?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:113/q14/p1", "position": "The augmentative min makes the negation universal, excluding even the smallest harm.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan and Samīn emphasize little or great; Alusi calls shayʾ an accusative cognate object in sense; Ibn Ashur says it is genitive after min but originally an absolute object; Baydawi describes cognate extent."}, {"id": "4:113/q14/p2", "position": "Ḍarr can mean diminution or reduction.", "reasons": "Damghani compares 3:111."}]}
{"id": "4:113/q15", "question": "What is the grammatical relation of 'God sent down the Book and Wisdom' to the preceding clause?", "turns_on": "Whether the waw starts a new favor, marks a circumstance, or supplies the protection's rationale.", "positions": [{"id": "4:113/q15/p1", "position": "The revelation clause supplies the reason that the plot cannot harm or mislead him.", "reasons": "Jishumi and Tabarsi invoke revelation of the Book and rulings; Razi connects scripture and conveyance of law with immunity from doubt; Ajhuri and Tabarsi are reported by Alusi; Abu Muslim rejects that explanatory link; Tabatabai grounds infallibility in revelation and teaching."}, {"id": "4:113/q15/p2", "position": "It begins a new coordinated statement of God's favor.", "reasons": "Wahidi and Qurtubi give the independent reading; Ibn Ashur says coordination reinforces the favor and sees an opening and closing ring."}, {"id": "4:113/q15/p3", "position": "The waw is circumstantial: they cannot harm him while God is sending revelation.", "reasons": "Wahidi supplies implicit qad and compares 4:90; Qurtubi cites Imru' al-Qays's birds-in-nests line; Tabatabai says it qualifies the apparently unrestricted denial of harm and notes grammarians' expected qad."}]}
